## Warm-up retrieval

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. A dataset is in *tidy* format when:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>It has no missing values</li>
  <li>Each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each observational unit has its own table</li>
  <li>The data is sorted alphabetically</li>
  <li>The column names are in lowercase</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Tidy data is about *structure*, not contents. Wickham's three rules are: variables in columns, observations in rows, observational units in their own tables. Tidy is unrelated to whether data is &quot;clean&quot; (free of errors or missing values).</div>
:::


## What you'll be able to do

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Conduct an exploratory data analysis (EDA) of a relationship between two numerical variables
- Fit a simple linear regression model with `lm()` and read its coefficients
- Interpret the *slope* and *intercept* of a fitted regression line in plain language
- Compute fitted values and *residuals* using `get_regression_points()` from `moderndive`

::: {.predict}
Before we begin: which of these objectives feels least familiar to you right now? Hold that in mind — we'll check back at the end.
:::

## Check-in: One numerical explanatory variable

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. In the model `lm(life_exp ~ fert_rate, data = UN_data_ch5)`, what does the *slope* coefficient represent?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The expected `life_exp` when `fert_rate` is 0</li>
  <li>The expected change in `life_exp` for a one-unit increase in `fert_rate`</li>
  <li>The total variance in `life_exp`</li>
  <li>The correlation between the two variables</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Slope = expected change in $y$ per one-unit change in $x$. The intercept (option a) is the predicted $y$ when $x = 0$.</div>
:::

Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q2. A *residual* is:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The slope of the fitted line</li>
  <li>The squared error of the model</li>
  <li>The vertical distance from an observed point to the fitted line: $y_i - \hat{y}_i$</li>
  <li>The R-squared value</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$. Small residuals (in aggregate) suggest the model fits well.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Related topics

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q3. A correlation coefficient of $r = -0.78$ between two variables means:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The relationship is causal</li>
  <li>There is a strong, *negative* linear relationship</li>
  <li>The variables are unrelated</li>
  <li>The variables have a perfect linear relationship</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Negative sign = inverse relationship; $|r|$ close to 1 = strong. Causation requires a randomized experiment or careful confounding adjustment, not just a strong correlation.</div>
:::
